module-1: The Home button (or swipe-up on newer iPads) is your Escape Hatch — pressing it once returns you to your familiar Home screen no matter what appears on screen, including scary pop-up warnings.
You cannot break your iPad by tapping the wrong thing. Every action on your device can be closed, undone, or ignored, and your device is built to be forgiving for everyday use.
To close a frozen app, double-press the Home button (or swipe up and pause on newer iPads) to see open apps as cards, then swipe the frozen app upward off the screen.
module-2: Use the 3-Second Rule every time something feels off: Stop — Breathe — Verify. Pausing before acting is the single most powerful defence against scams.
No real government agency, including the CRA, will ever demand payment by gift card, Bitcoin, prepaid card, or wire transfer. Any request for these payment methods is always a scam.
If you think you have been targeted by a scam, call the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501. Reporting the scam is not embarrassing — it protects other Canadians.
module-2.5: Before sending any Interac e-Transfer, double-check the recipient's email address character by character — once accepted, a transfer cannot be cancelled.

You can book Ontario doctor and specialist appointments online through your clinic's patient portal or MyChart. Always verify the website address starts with your clinic's real domain before entering your health card number.
Turning on Automatic Updates (Settings → App Store → App Updates, and Settings → General → Software Update → Automatic Updates) keeps your device secure without any effort on your part.
module-3: A strong passphrase — three or four random words strung together, such as 'purple-lamp-harbour-78' — is both easier to remember and harder for criminals to crack than a short jumbled password.
Never use the same password for more than one account. If one account is stolen, attackers immediately try the same password on your bank, email, and social media accounts.
Face ID and Touch ID are safe: your biometric data never leaves your device and is never sent to Apple or stored anywhere outside your phone or tablet.
module-4: Only ever download apps from the official App Store (Apple) or Google Play Store (Android). Never install an app from a link sent by text or email, no matter who appears to have sent it.

Before tapping Get, check that the app has thousands of reviews and that the developer name matches the real company you expect — scammers create convincing lookalike apps with nearly identical names.

If you are unsure about any permission an app requests — such as access to your contacts, camera, or location — choose Don't Allow. You can always change this later in Settings, and refusing does not break the app.
module-5: Never tap a link in an email asking you to verify your account or confirm your identity. Legitimate companies never ask for this by email — if concerned, go directly to their website by typing the address yourself.
Check the sender's full email address, not just the display name. Scammers use addresses that look almost right, such as 'support@rbc-secure-alerts.com' instead of the genuine rbc.com domain.
Scam text messages claiming to be from Canada Post, your bank, or a delivery service are very common in Canada. Delete any text with a suspicious link without tapping it.
module-6: Your bank will never phone, email, or text you to ask for your password, PIN, or security questions. If anyone contacts you asking for these, hang up and call your bank using the number on the back of your card.
When shopping or banking online, always check that the web address starts with https:// and look for the padlock icon in the address bar before entering any payment or personal details.
Always sign out fully when you finish online banking — especially on a shared or public computer. Simply closing the browser window is not enough to protect your session.
module-7: Turning on iCloud Photos (Settings → your name → iCloud → Photos) backs up every photo and video automatically — they are safe even if your iPad is lost, stolen, damaged, or replaced.
Deleting a photo does not remove it permanently straight away — it moves to Recently Deleted and stays there for 30 days, giving you plenty of time to recover anything deleted by mistake.
You can share a photo album with specific family members without giving anyone access to your entire library — use the Shared Albums feature in Photos to control exactly who sees what.
module-8: FaceTime is free, already installed on every iPhone and iPad, and requires no account beyond your Apple ID — just open it and tap a contact to start a video call.
For the clearest video calls, prop your iPad at eye level (a cookbook stand works perfectly), sit facing a window so natural light falls on your face, and connect to Wi-Fi if possible.
Only add people you know and trust to group messages and shared photo albums. If you receive a group invitation from someone you do not recognise, do not join it — block and delete it.
module-9: AI tools like ChatGPT or Siri can be very helpful but can also make confident mistakes. Always double-check important information about health, legal matters, or finances with a trusted source.
Never share personal information with any AI chat tool: no Social Insurance Number, banking details, passwords, home address, or medical details. Your conversations may be stored and reviewed.
If you receive a call or video message from a family member urgently asking for money, hang up and call that person back on their regular number — AI can now convincingly clone voices and faces.
module-10: Apps such as PC Express, Instacart, and Uber Eats show you the full cost — including delivery fee, tips, and taxes — before you confirm your order. You are never charged before you say yes.
Review your order carefully before tapping Place Order: check quantities, substitution preferences, delivery address, and the total cost including all fees.
Your payment information in grocery and food delivery apps is protected with the same bank-level encryption used by major Canadian retailers.
module-11: Before getting into any ride-share vehicle, do three safety checks: confirm the driver's name matches the app, confirm the licence plate matches, and confirm the driver says your first name without prompting.
If anything does not match — wrong plate, driver unsure of your name, or anything feels off — do NOT get in. Cancel the trip in the app and request a new driver. Your safety comes first.
Uber and Lyft confirm the price before you book, so there are no surprise fares. You can also share your live trip details with a family member directly from inside the app.
module-12: When stuck in an automated phone menu, say 'representative' or 'agent' clearly, or press 0 — this usually connects you to a real person faster than navigating every menu option.

Never allow remote access to your device if someone called you unexpectedly — even if the caller ID shows Apple, Microsoft, or your bank. Caller ID can be faked. Hang up and call the company back yourself.
Free, patient tech support is available to Canadian seniors at no cost: Connected Canadians 1-855-808-0505 and Cyber-Seniors 1-844-217-3057 both offer bilingual telephone assistance.
module-13: Set your Facebook privacy to Friends Only so strangers cannot see your posts: tap the three-line menu → Settings → Privacy → Who can see your future posts? → Friends.
Never send money to someone you have met only online, regardless of how convincing their story sounds. Romance scams cost Canadians over $50 million every year — the rule is absolute: no money.
If anyone on Facebook Marketplace or Instagram asks you to pay using gift cards, stop immediately. No legitimate seller ever requests gift cards — it is always a scam.
module-14: Smart plugs are the safest and easiest starting point for a smart home — they cost $15–$30, plug into any outlet, and let you control any lamp or appliance by voice or app.
Use a strong Wi-Fi password (at least 12 characters, not your address or birthday) for all smart home devices. Your internet provider can help you change it if needed.
Every voice assistant (Alexa, Google Home, Siri) has a physical mute button that stops it from listening. A red light confirms the microphone is off. You control when it listens.
module-15: Most telehealth video or phone appointments with your Ontario family doctor are covered by OHIP at no cost — the same as an in-person visit. Ask your clinic if virtual appointments are available.
Ontario's free 24/7 nurse advice line (1-866-797-0000) connects you with a registered nurse at any hour — evenings, weekends, and holidays included.
For your video appointment, sit in a quiet well-lit room, test your camera and microphone a few minutes early, and have your health card and a list of current medications ready.
module-16: Back up all your photos and important documents to iCloud before you travel — if your device is lost or stolen, everything is recoverable when you get home.
Avoid using public Wi-Fi at airports, hotels, and coffee shops for banking, email, or personal accounts. Use your phone's cellular data instead, or a VPN if you have one.
Keep a printed copy of your passport photo page, travel insurance policy number, and emergency contact numbers in a separate bag from your passport and main luggage.
module-17: AI tools can answer questions and help you draft text — but they sometimes state incorrect information confidently. Always verify important facts with a second trusted source.
Never share your Social Insurance Number, banking details, passwords, or home address with any AI chat tool. Your conversations may be stored on external servers.
A good prompt habit: tell the AI who you are and what you need — 'I am a Canadian senior looking for simple instructions on how to...' — to get clearer, more relevant answers.
module-18: FaceTime requires no special setup beyond an Apple ID — tap the app, tap a contact's name, and tap Video. You can hang up at any time by pressing the red button.
Friendly Voices (1-855-892-5446) is a free Canadian service that matches seniors with a trained volunteer for regular friendly phone conversations — no internet required.
Many Ontario public libraries run free digital programmes: Zoom clubs, tech help sessions, and interest-based online groups. Ask at your local branch what is available.
module-19: Make a written list of your important online accounts — email, banking, social media — and store it securely with your will or in a sealed envelope with your estate documents. This is a practical gift to your family.
Facebook lets you appoint a Legacy Contact (Settings → General → Memorialisation Settings) who can manage your account and post a tribute after you pass away.

Photos stored in iCloud or on an external drive are part of your digital estate. Decide now who you want to receive them, and include those instructions in your will or with your estate planning documents.
